$comment: The curriculum spine. Drives scripts/gen.mjs (images, via gpt-image-bridge → gpt-image-2) and scripts/yt.mjs (video curation). Ordered as a learning path, not a reference index. 'authored' entries are diagrams a human must draw — deliberately NOT generatable; see content/visual-grammar.md §5. Image prompts are dense on purpose: gpt-image-2 takes no reference images here, so the text carries all style consistency.

concepts.title: The Four Forces
concepts.oneLiner: Everything an aircraft does is four arrows arguing with each other.
concepts.misconception: That the four forces are always balanced. They are balanced only in unaccelerated flight — which is the boring case.
concepts.concrete: A paper plane thrown across a room, slowing and sinking.
videoQueries: four forces of flight explained lift weight thrust drag
forces on an aircraft in steady level flight explained

images.prompt:
Subject: a single small high-wing propeller aircraft, rendered as a clean flat slate silhouette with the fuselage and wing separated into two tones of deep blue and mid blue. Seen from directly abeam, perfectly level, nose to the left. Propeller disc suggested as a soft translucent bone ellipse.
Setting: empty sky. One soft vertical wash from mid blue at the top to paper at the horizon. A single flat bone cloud bank sitting low, far below the aircraft.
Composition: aircraft centred on the upper-middle third, occupying about 35% of the frame width. Vast quiet paper above and below it. Horizon line low, level, unbroken.
Colour: paper dominant. Amber used only for a single thin stripe along the fuselage.
Mood: calm, suspended, contemplative — a machine held in equilibrium.

authored: Free-body diagram, 4 states: (1) aircraft alone, (2) +weight, (3) +lift, (4) +thrust and drag.
Same diagram in a climb, showing why lift is NOT equal to weight.

diagrams.shows: Steady level flight: all four forces equal and balanced.
Steady climb: L = W cos γ so L < W, and T > D. Derives it by resolving weight across the flight path.

concepts.secondMisconception: That climbing needs more lift. It needs more thrust — lift actually decreases, because lift answers to the flight path and only has to balance W cos γ.

concepts.title: Where Lift Actually Comes From
concepts.oneLiner: The wing throws air downward. Newton's third law does the rest.
concepts.misconception: Equal transit time — that air separating at the leading edge must rejoin at the trailing edge, so the longer top path forces faster flow. It doesn't rejoin, and the explanation predicts that inverted flight is impossible. It is not.
concepts.concrete: A hand held flat out of a moving car window, tilted.
videoQueries: how airplane wings really generate lift
lift explained Newton third law downwash not Bernoulli
why the equal transit time explanation of lift is wrong

images.prompt:
Subject: a single airfoil cross-section — a smooth asymmetric wing profile, thick rounded leading edge tapering to a fine trailing edge — floating alone in still air, tilted about eight degrees nose-up. Solid deep blue with a slate outline. Beneath and behind it, three or four long flat bone ribbons curve gently downward, suggesting deflected air, drawn as smooth solid shapes rather than lines.

Mood: quiet, weightless, forensic.

authored: Side-by-side: the wrong model (parcels rejoining) vs measured flow (they never rejoin). This figure is the whole lesson.
Downwash + reaction force, 3 states.
Inverted flight as the falsification test.

concepts.title: Angle of Attack, and the Cliff at the End
concepts.oneLiner: More angle means more lift — right up until the air stops following the wing.
concepts.misconception: That a stall is caused by flying too slowly. A wing stalls at one angle of attack, at any speed, in any attitude.
concepts.concrete: Tilting a spoon under a running tap until the water breaks away.
videoQueries: angle of attack and stall explained smoke tunnel flow separation
why a wing stalls at any airspeed critical angle of attack
boundary layer separation airfoil visualization

images.prompt:
Subject: a horizontal band of flow reading left to right across the frame, rendered as roughly a dozen long flat parallel ribbons in mid blue. On the left they run smooth, straight and evenly spaced. Around two thirds of the way across they lift, thicken, and break apart into a field of loose rounded bone and amber shapes tumbling upward — ordered flow becoming chaos. No wing, no aircraft, no object causing it.
Setting: plain paper ground, nothing else.
Composition: the band occupies the central third of the frame height and runs the full width. The break point sits at the golden ratio, about 62% across. Wide empty paper above and below the band.
Colour: mid blue for the ordered ribbons, bone for the turbulent shapes, amber on only two or three of the tumbling forms at the break.

concepts.title: Two Kinds of Drag, Pulling Opposite Ways
concepts.oneLiner: Going faster costs you one kind of drag and saves you the other. The best speed is where they cross.
concepts.misconception: That flying slower always saves fuel. Below best-L/D speed, slowing down costs more — the back side of the drag curve.
concepts.concrete: Wading through water: slow is easy, fast is exhausting — but standing still in a current is its own problem.
videoQueries: induced drag versus parasite drag explained total drag curve
region of reverse command back side of the power curve
lift to drag ratio best glide speed explained

concepts.title: Three Axes, Three Controls
concepts.oneLiner: Roll, pitch, yaw — and the three surfaces that command them.
concepts.misconception: That the rudder turns the aircraft. It does not; the bank angle does. The rudder coordinates the turn.
concepts.concrete: A hand held flat, rotating about three imaginary skewers through the palm.
videoQueries: roll pitch yaw axes explained aircraft control surfaces

images.prompt:
Subject: a simplified aircraft form — swept wing, clean fuselage, T-tail — seen from a shallow three-quarter view from above and slightly ahead, sitting perfectly level. The form is a smooth, uninterrupted, featureless solid — absolutely no windows, no doors, no panel lines, no rivets, no engine intakes, no surface detail of any kind. Built from hard-edged flat colour fills with no outline at all: deep blue upper surfaces meeting mid blue directly where a plane turns away from the light, the colour boundary itself doing the drawing. No pencil or crayon texture, no sketchy or wobbly linework, no ink contour, no soft airbrush shading or gradients anywhere on the body.
Setting: plain paper ground with a single flat bone shadow shape offset down and to the right of the aircraft, hard-edged.
Composition: aircraft centred, nose toward the lower left, occupying about 40% of the frame width. Even paper margin on all four sides. Nothing touches the frame edge.
Colour: paper dominant, deep and mid blue for the airframe, bone for the shadow, and one small amber accent at the very tip of the vertical tail fin.
Mood: precise, specimen-like, diagrammatic calm.

authored: The three axes through the CG — the canonical figure the whole project references later.
Each control surface deflecting, with the resulting moment arrow, 3 separate figures sharing one viewBox.

concepts.title: Why an Aircraft Wants to Fly Level
concepts.oneLiner: Stability is what happens when a disturbance produces a force that undoes it.
concepts.misconception: That stability and controllability are the same thing. They trade against each other — a fighter is deliberately less stable so it can be more controllable.
concepts.concrete: A marble in a bowl versus a marble on an upturned bowl.
videoQueries: static stability aircraft explained centre of gravity neutral point
static margin explained aircraft stability
why the horizontal stabilizer pushes down

The basin is drawn as one clean flat curve in mid blue, its interior filled bone, sitting on a plain surface. A hard-edged bone shadow sits directly under the sphere. Nothing else — no hands, no aircraft, no motion lines.

concepts.title: The Two Ways an Aircraft Bobs
concepts.oneLiner: Disturb the pitch and you get a fast, sharp wobble and a slow, lazy swoop — at the same time.
concepts.misconception: That these are pilot-induced. They are the aircraft's own natural modes; they exist with the controls locked.
concepts.concrete: A boat: the quick chop and the long swell are separate motions superimposed.
videoQueries: phugoid mode explained aircraft dynamic stability
short period oscillation aircraft longitudinal dynamics
aircraft dynamic modes demonstration flight test

The other is a fast, tight, small-amplitude wave in deep blue riding exactly along the first one's path. Both fade out at the left and right edges by breaking into a few separated flat segments rather than being cropped.

concepts.title: Dutch Roll, Spiral, and Roll Damping
concepts.oneLiner: Three more natural motions — one of which is why your coffee slides sideways.
concepts.misconception: That the spiral mode being unstable is a design flaw. It is a deliberate trade; a spirally-stable aircraft is unpleasantly stiff in roll.
concepts.concrete: A shopping trolley with one bad wheel: it wanders, it wags, and it resists being pushed sideways.

concepts.title: Turning Costs You
concepts.oneLiner: A turn is a controlled fall sideways, and it makes you heavier.
concepts.misconception: That a steeper turn is dangerous because of the angle. It is dangerous because load factor raises stall speed — a 60° bank doubles your effective weight and raises stall speed by 41%.
concepts.concrete: Leaning into a corner on a bicycle; the push you feel through the seat.
videoQueries: load factor in a turn explained stall speed increase bank angle
why a level turn requires more lift explained
accelerated stall explained turning flight

concepts.title: The Envelope, and Its Corners
concepts.oneLiner: There is a speed below which you fall and above which you break. The gap narrows with altitude.
concepts.misconception: That high altitude is uniformly safer because there is more room. At the coffin corner, stall speed and critical Mach converge to nearly a single speed.
concepts.concrete: A doorway that narrows as you walk toward it.
videoQueries: coffin corner explained high altitude flight envelope
critical mach number explained transonic drag rise
flight envelope explained aircraft limits

Below the arc, a flat bone field of cloud tops, drawn as three or four overlapping soft shapes. No aircraft anywhere.

concepts.title: Six Numbers That Describe Everything
concepts.oneLiner: Three translations, three rotations. Every motion an aircraft can make is a combination of six.
concepts.misconception: That the equations are the hard part. The equations are Newton's laws in a rotating frame; the hard part is the aerodynamic coefficients that feed them.
concepts.concrete: Describing where a bee is and which way it is pointing — that's six numbers, and nothing else is needed.

concepts.title: Closing the Loop
